topics.title: Massive Hemorrhage / MTP
topics.subtitle: Shock, active bleeding, falling hemoglobin, coagulopathy, transfusion need

sections.title: Acute Management
items: Airway: if AMS, massive hematemesis, or hemodynamic collapse: intubate early; RSI with hemodynamically neutral agents (ketamine, avoid propofol in shock)
Breathing: SpO2, supplemental O2; monitor for aspiration if upper GI source
Circulation: 2 largebore IVs (≥16G), IO, or rapid infuser access; start crystalloid wide open while blood products prepared
Activate MTP now: do NOT wait for labs to confirm hemorrhage if clinical picture is clear
Transfuse Oneg or uncrossmatched pRBCs while type & cross pending

sections.title: PostMTP assessment
items: Repeat MTP labs: CBC, coags, fibrinogen, iCa, ABG
Check pt temp: treat hypothermia
POCUS to check volume status: flat IVC may indicate continued hemorrhage vs overresuscitation
Correct electrolyte abnormalities (calcium, potassium, magnesium)
Platelet & coagulation factor targets depend on hemostasis security: if definitive hemostasis achieved (IR embolization), repletion less critical; if tenuous, target more robust coag parameters
Fibrinogen >150-200, INR <1.5, platelets >50k (>100k for CNS or ocular bleeding), iCa >1.1, temp >35, pH >7.2

sections.title: When to Activate MTP
items: >5 units PBCs within 4 hours
Active hemorrhage with hemodynamic instability (SBP <90, HR >120)
on pressors
ruptured AAA, massive GIB, Ob bleed
Do NOT use hemoglobin to trigger MTP: Hgb takes hours to fall after hemorrhage
If doubt exists whether the pt is in hemorrhagic shock: bedside echo to confirm hypovolemia

pairs.value: 1:1:1: pRBC: FFP: Platelets.
Consider 1:1:1:1 adding cryoprecipitate for prolonged MTP. Give 10 units cryo if fibrinogen <150-200 mg/dL. inc ↑fibrinogen ~75 mg/dL / 10 units.
Saline & LR dilute clotting factors & do nothing to stop hemorrhage. Blood products only for hemorrhagic shock resuscitation.
Target MAP 50-60 mmHg until hemostasis achieved. Overresuscitation dislodges clots & worsens venous bleeding (esp variceal). Exception: TBI: target higher MAP.
Multiple 16-18G peripheral IVs: adequate with Belmont pressure infuser (300-500 mL/min).
Rapid Infusion Cater: 7Fr placed via Seldinger through existing PIV. Equivalent to 13.3G. Best option for largebore peripheral access. NOT pressureinjectable (no CT contrast).
Ultrasoundguided access above medial malleolus. Large,pristine vein. Distend with tourniquet + Trendelenburg. Good option when arm veins are collapsed or damaged.
Acceptable but lower flow rates. Remove line cap before attaching pressure infuser. Use largest lumen. Most are pressureinjectable for CT.
Introducer sheaths: high failure rate, kink without catheter in place. Hemodialysis catheter NOT pressureinjectable.
Place early for BP monitoring. Femoral artery + femoral vein on same side (dirty double) is fastest way to get both simultaneously.

sections.title: MTP Labs (q30-60 min)
items: CBC: trending Hgb & platelets
Coags: INR, PTT, fibrinogen
AntiXa level if on heparin or oral Xa inhibitor
TEG (if avail): guides fibrinogen, antifibrinolytic, & platelet therapy in real time
Electrolytes + ionized calcium (iCa): follow closely during MTP
ABG/VBG: monitor pH, avoid acidosis
Type & crossmatch: already be done before MTP activation

sections.title: Management
items: Goal 1:1:1 ratio (pRBCs: FFP: platelets); give TXA 1 g IV over 10 min within first 3 hrs of hemorrhage
check & treat lethal triad: hypothermia (warm fluids, blankets), acidosis (resuscitate, limit crystalloid), coagulopathy (blood products, TXA, factor replacement)
Permissive ↓ BP: target SBP 80-90 mmHg or MAP ~50-60 until source control achieved. Exception: TBI, spinal cord ischemia, or pregnancy may require higher targets
Use blood products, not liters of crystalloid, as the primary resuscitation fluid once hemorrhagic shock is recognized
Replace fibrinogen early: cryoprecipitate if fibrinogen <150-200 mg/dL or if prolonged MTP suggests depletion
Replace calcium aggressively during MTP; citrate load from products causes hypocalcemia & worsens coagulopathy
Reverse pre-existing anticoagulation / coagulopathy: PCC + vitamin K for warfarin, specific DOAC reversal when indicated, protamine for heparin
Identify source & achieve source control: surgical consult, GI for endoscopy, IR for embolization, OB for postpartum hemorrhage
Do not chase a normal hemoglobin early: hemodynamics, transfusion requirement, bedside exam, & response to products matter more in the first hours

pairs.value: Tranexamic acid (TXA) 1g over 10 min then 1g over 8h: give within 3h of injury. Indications: trauma, obstetric hemorrhage, TEG LY30 >3%, cirrhosis with hyperfibrinolysis.
Cryoprecipitate if fibrinogen <150-200 mg/dL. Fibrinogen is first factor to reach critically low levels in massive hemorrhage.
1-2g CaCl2 OR 3-6g calcium gluconate per MTP round (every 6 units pRBC). Target iCa 1.1-1.3 mM. Citrate in blood products chelates calcium: hypocalcemia causes coagulopathy.
0.3 mcg/kg IV (max 21 mcg). Consider if: renal failure, thrombocytopenia, or antiplatelet drugs.
MTP will not correct pre-existing coagulopathy. Reverse warfarin (PCC + Vit K), DOACs (&exanet/idarucizumab), heparin (protamine) independently.
Target nl. pH. Even mild acidosis (pH 7.20) substantially impairs coagulation cascade. Correct with bicarb if needed.
Use warmed blood products (Level1 or Belmont infusers with inline warming). Forcedair warming blanket. Monitor core temp ly.
Prioritize fastest strategy: IR embolization or surgical packing over definitive repair.Don't delay source control for resuscitation optimization.

drugs.name: Tranexamic acid (TXA)
drugs.notes: Give within 3h of injury. Trauma & obstetric hemorrhage. Aminocaproic acid 4-5g load then 1g/hr is an alternative.

drugs.name: Calcium chloride (CaCl2)
drugs.dose: 1-2g IV per MTP round (6 units pRBC)
drugs.notes: Preferred if central access available. Peripheral extravasation causes tissue necrosis: use calcium gluconate for peripheral lines.

drugs.name: Calcium gluconate
drugs.notes: Safe for peripheral administration. Target iCa 1.1-1.3 mM. Replace routinely —don't wait for sx.

drugs.name: Cryoprecipitate
drugs.notes: Give if fibrinogen <150-200 mg/dL. Consider empiric 1:1:1:1 ratio (adding cryo) for prolonged MTP.

drugs.name: DDAVP (desmopressin)
drugs.notes: Promotes platelet function. Use if renal failure, thrombocytopenia, or on antiplatelet agents.

drugs.name: 4factor PCC (Kcentra)
drugs.notes: Warfarin reversal: faster than FFP. Always give with Vitamin K 10mg IV to prevent rebound.

drugs.name: Sodium bicarbonate
drugs.notes: Correct acidosis: pH <7.2 substantially impairs coagulation. Target nl. pH during MTP.

topics.title: Anticoagulation Reversal
topics.subtitle: Major bleeding, suprathetherapeutic anticoagulation, urgent procedure, intracranial hemorrhage

sections.title: Acute Management
items: Airway: check patency and protect. Breathing: check WOB, oxygenation, and ventilation. Circulation: check pulse, BP, perfusion, and IV access.
Do NOT delay reversal for labs if life-threatening hemorrhage: give empiric reversal based on known agent

sections.title: Chart Check / Hx.
items: IDanticoagulant, dose, indication, & time of last dose: this determines if reversal is still useful
Clarify bleeding site & severity: ICH, GI bleed, retroperitoneal, airway, pericardial, intraocular, postop, traumatic
Ask whether the issue is major bleeding, clinically relevant nonmajor bleeding, or urgent surgery / procedure
Renal & hepatic function matter: DOAC clearance is prolonged in CKD / liver disease
Review concomitant agents: aspirin, clopidogrel, ticagrelor, NSAIDs, SSRIs, thrombolytics
For warfarin: check baseline INR trend, diet changes, antibiotics, amiodarone, liver disease, alcohol use
For heparin / LMWH: determine when it was started, infusion rate, bolus timing, & recent procedures
Look for thrombotic indication & risk if held: mechanical valve, recent VTE, LV thrombus, AFib with prior stroke

sections.title: Exam
items: Airway & neuro status first: headache, vomiting, focal deficit, declining GCS, neck swelling, stridor
Hemodynamics: tachycardia, hypotension, perfusion, orthostasis, shock
Look for occult bleeding: flank / back ecchymosis, abd distension, melena, hematuria, large hematomas, joint swelling
Skin / access sites: expanding IV site hematoma, surgical drains, catheter sites, ecchymoses
Remember: anticoagulant level / INR DOESN'T predict bleeding severity: treat pt & source

sections.title: Management
items: Identify anticoagulant: warfarin, heparin, enoxaparin, rivaroxaban, apixaban, dabigatran, etc.
Hold ALL anticoagulants & antiplatelets now
Control source: endoscopy, IR embolization, surgery, neurosurgery, ENT, bronchoscopy, compression / packing
Transfuse blood products as clinically indicated; reversal agents don't replace standard hemorrhage resuscitation
For warfarin: 4factor PCC (Kcentra) 25-50 units/kg IV + vitamin K 10 mg IV (PCC works in minutes; vitamin K takes 6-24 hrs)
For dabigatran: idarucizumab (Praxbind) 5 g IV
For rivaroxaban/apixaban: &exanet alfa (&exxa) or 4factor PCC 50 units/kg if &exanet unavailable
For heparin: protamine sulfate 1 mg per 100 units heparin given in last 2-3 hrs (max 50 mg)
If bleeding is not life-threatening & the last dose was remote, supportive care + temporary drug hold may safer than full reversal
Repeat reassessment after reversal: vitals, bleeding exam, Hgmb trend, & whether source control has been achieved
Recheck coag parameters after intervention: INR after warfarin reversal, aPTT / antiXa, fibrinogen if massively bleeding
Watch for rebound anticoagulation or continued bleeding: especially after vitamin K is omitted, PCC wears off, or dabigatran redistributes
Monitor for thrombosis after PCC / &exanet / factor products, particularly in recent VTE, ACS, stroke, or mechanical valve pts
Develop a reanticoagulation plan post hemostasis. thrombosis risk returns quickly in some pts

pairs.value: 4factor PCC (Kcentra) for urgent reversal + Vitamin K 10mg IV. FFP if PCC unavailable.
Protamine sulfate 1mg per 100 units heparin given in last 2-3h. Max 50mg.
Protamine 1mg per 1mg enoxaparin if <8h since last dose. Partial reversal if >8h.
4factor PCC 50 units/kg.
Idarucizumab (Praxbind) 5g IV: complete reversal. Dialyzable as backup.
No specific antidote. Supportive care; consider PCC / aPCC in life-threatening bleeding after specialist discussion
No specific antidote. Stop infusion; short halflife means effect falls quickly, but may prolonged in organ dysfunction
Reverse only for true major bleeding / critical procedures. Restart planning matters early: discuss with cardiology / hematology
CBC, PT/INR, aPTT, fibrinogen, CMP / Cr, type & screen, lactate if unstable
AntiXa level if avail for apixaban / rivaroxaban or LMWH; thrombin time for dabigatran; heparin antiXa / aPTT for UFH
CT head for neuro sx or trauma, CTA / endoscopy / bronchoscopy / IR imaging based on suspected source
Serial Hgb / Hct q4-6h in active bleed, telemetry if unstable, strict I&Os, neuro checks if CNS bleed suspected
Pharmacy, hematology, IR / surgery / GI / neurosurgery depending on bleed site; cardiology if mechanical valve or extreme thrombotic risk

drugs.name: 4factor PCC (Kcentra)
drugs.notes: Fastest warfarin reversal. Always give with Vitamin K to prevent rebound.

drugs.name: Vitamin K (phytonadione)
drugs.notes: Sustained warfarin reversal (effect in 6-24h). Always give with PCC for urgent reversal.

drugs.name: Protamine sulfate
drugs.notes: Give slowly over 10 min: rapid infusion causes ↓ BP. Monitor for anaphylaxis.

drugs.name: Idarucizumab (Praxbind)
drugs.notes: Dabigatran reversal. Immediate reversal.

drugs.name: &andexanet alfa
drugs.dose: Low dose: 400mg bolus + 480mg over 2h; High dose: 800mg bolus + 960mg over 2h
drugs.notes: Reverses rivaroxaban, apixaban. High dose for rivaroxaban >10mg or apixaban >5mg taken <8h prior.

drugs.name: FFP
drugs.notes: Use if PCC unavailable for warfarin reversal or if broader factor replacement is needed. Slower & largervolume than PCC.

drugs.name: Tranexamic acid (TXA)
drugs.dose: 1g IV over 10 min, then 1g over 8h when appropriate
drugs.contraindications: Active intravascular clotting; caution in hematuria / upper urinary tract bleeding
drugs.notes: Adjunctive hemostatic thetherapy for selected trauma, postop, mucosal, or postpartum bleeding. Not an anticoagulant antidote.

pairs.value: persistent respiratory distress, high-flow or NIV need, hemodynamic instability, vasopressor need, severe arrhythmia, airway risk, neurologic decline, or a trajectory suggesting pt may crash on the floor.

topics.title: Bloodless Medicine / Jehovah's Witness
topics.subtitle: Severe anemia, bleeding risk, transfusion refusal, hypoperfusion signs

sections.title: Acute Management
items: Airway: check patency and protect. Breathing: check WOB, oxygenation, and ventilation. Circulation: check pulse, BP, perfusion, and IV access.
Control bleeding now: source control, procedural hemostasis, surgery, IR, OB/GI intervention, & local/topical hemostatic measures.
Minimize iatrogenic blood loss: pediatric tubes, bundle labs, point of care testing, & bloodconservation sampling devices when available.
Support oxygen delivery: supplemental oxygen, optimize preload & perfusion, treat fever, treat shock, & avoid unnecessary hemodilution.

sections.title: Chart Check / Hx.
items: What is specifically refused: packed RBCs, plasma, platelets, cryoprecipitate, albumin, cell salvage, acute normovolemic hemodilution, clotting factor concentrates, PCC, recombinant factor VIIa, etc.
Baseline hemoglobin, trajectory, active bleeding source, hemodynamic stability, & signs of endorgan ischemia.
Current anticoagulants / antiplatelets & last dose.
Iron deficiency, CKD, malignancy, infection, or nutritional deficiency that may limit erythropoiesis.
Prior documentation, advance directives, blood refusal card, durable power of attorney, or prior bloodless medicine plan.

sections.title: Exam
items: Vitals/perfusion: tachycardia, ↓ BP, cool extremities, delayed cap refill, shock
Look for active blood loss: melena, hematemesis, hematuria, vaginal bleeding, drain output, expanding hematoma
Signs of critical anemia: chest pain, dyspnea, syncope, AMS, ischemic EKG changes, low UOP, rising lactate
check volume status: severe anemia may coexist with hemorrhagic shock or dilution from excess IVF
Document neuro, cardiopulm, & airway findings if the bleed location could worsen quickly

pairs.value: Care strategy that respects transfusion refusal while maximizing hemostasis, oxygen delivery, & erythropoiesis.
Acceptance of fractions or bloodconservation techniques is individualized. Ask & document exactly what is acceptable.
No single cutoff, but risk rises sharply as Hgb approaches <5-6 g/dL, especially with bleeding, shock, sepsis, or ischemia.
Whole blood & primary blood components such as RBCs, plasma, platelets, & WBCs are commonly refused.

Some pts may accept minor fractions or procedures that maintain continuity with body, such as clotting factors, PCC, recombinant factor VIIa, albumin, cell salvage, or acute normovolemic hemodilution. Individual preference matters.
Never assume acceptance or refusal of fractionated product or bloodconservation technique without asking pt.
Mortality rises sharply as hemoglobin falls into <5-6 g/dL range, especially with bleeding, shock, ischemia, or sepsis.
Stop bleeding, reduce oxygen consumption, optimize perfusion, & stimulate erythropoiesis early.
Hemoglobinbased oxygen carriers may considered in extreme, life-threatening anemia where available, but access is limited &requires emergency regulatory processes.

sections.title: Blood Conservation Strategies
items: Use pediatric / lowvolume phlebotomy tubes for all draws.
Order only essential labs & avoid repetitive "routine" blood work.
Use point of care testing when it decreases total blood loss.
If pt accepts it, consider cell salvage or autologous techniques for surgical/procedural blood loss.
Avoid unnecessary IV fluids once initial resuscitation is complete: excessive crystalloid worsens hemodilution.
Treat fever, agitation, pain, & shivering to reduce oxygen demand.

drugs.name: Epoetin alfa
drugs.dose: 20,000-30,000 units IV daily to every or day OR 40,000 units daily until Hgb >7 g/dL, then weekly
drugs.contraindications: Uncontrolled severe HTN, history of ESA hypersensitivity; use caution with thrombosis risk
drugs.notes: Stimulates erythropoiesis. Effect is not immediate; reticulocyte response begins after several days. Requires adequate iron support.

drugs.name: Iron sucrose
drugs.dose: 100-200 mg IV daily for several days (commonly 3-10 days depending on severity & iron status)
drugs.contraindications: Prior iron hypersensitivity; caution with active infection
drugs.notes: Useful when iron deficiency is present or suspected, or when rapid support of erythropoiesis is needed. Oral iron is slower.

drugs.name: Folate
drugs.notes: Supportive vitamin supplementation to maximize erythropoiesis.

drugs.name: Vitamin B12
drugs.dose: Per deficiency protocol or daily supplementation if deficiency status is unclear
drugs.notes: Correct deficiency or empirically supplement when erythropoietic support is being pursued.

drugs.name: Vitamin C
drugs.notes: Often used as an adjunct with iron therapy in bloodless anemia protocols.

drugs.name: Tranexamic acid
drugs.dose: 1 g IV over 10 min, then 1 g over 8 h for major bleeding when appropriate
drugs.contraindications: Active intravascular clotting; use indicationspecific caution
drugs.notes: Antifibrinolytic adjunct for trauma, procedural bleeding, postpartum hemorrhage, & selected mucosal bleeding states.

drugs.name: 4factor PCC (Kcentra)
drugs.dose: 25-50 units/kg IV depending on indication / INR
drugs.notes: Often acceptable to some Jehovah's Witness pts b/c it is blood fraction, but acceptance is individual. Useful for urgent warfarin or factorbased reversal.

drugs.name: Recombinant factor VIIa
drugs.notes: May be considered as rescue hemostatic adjunct in selected life-threatening bleeding cases if acceptable to pt.

pairs.value: Trauma, GI bleed, postpartum hemorrhage, operative/procedural bleeding, ruptured vascular source.
Iron deficiency, CKD, marrow suppression, malignancy, B12/folate deficiency, inflammation.
Autoimmune hemolysis, microangiopathy, drug induced hemolysis, mechanical hemolysis.
Repeated phlebotomy, excess crystalloid causing hemodilution, anticoagulation/antiplatelet effect.
Do not assume anemia alone: also consider sepsis, PE, ACS, tamponade, tension physiology, or occult hemorrhage.

sections.title: Management
items: Clarify goals & exactly what pt will or will not accept early. Document discussionin chart.
If pt has decisionmaking capacity, discuss blood products privately & directly with pt not relying only on family input.
Stop anticoagulants & antiplatelet agents when bleeding riskoutweighs benefit; reverse coagulopathy with acceptable agents.
Consult hematology, anesthesia, surgery/procedure team, pharmacy, ethics, & bloodless medicine services early if avail.

sections.title: Workup & Monitoring
items: CBC trend, reticulocyte count, ferritin, iron studies, B12, folate, CMP, hemolysis labs if needed.
Coags & fibrinogen when bleeding or coagulopathy is suspected.
Track perfusion & oxygen delivery: lactate, telemetry, chest pain symptoms, neuro status, urine output.
Recheck hemoglobin trend after limiting phlebotomy b/c act of monitoring worsens anemia.

pairs.value: CBC trend, retic, ferritin/iron studies, B12, folate, CMP, coags/fibrinogen, hemolysis labs if needed.
Telemetry, serial vitals, lactate, urine output, ischemic symptoms, & minimize repeat phlebotomy.
Sourcespecific imaging/endoscopy/procedural evaluation if active blood loss is suspected.
Record accepted and refused products, fractions, & procedures in a visible part of the chart.
Early heme, surgery/procedural team, anesthesia, pharmacy, ethics, & bloodless medicine service if avail.
In severe hemorrhage, definitive bleeding control matters more than any anemia adjunct.
Erythropoietin helps, but it is not an immediate rescue therapy: plan for lag of days before meaningful hemoglobin response.
IV iron is preferred over oral iron in severe inpt anemia or when rapid marrow support is needed.
Document accepted & refused therapies precisely so consultants, overnight teams, & procedural servicesdon't make assumptions.

topics.title: Coagulopathy Reversal
topics.subtitle: Elevated INR, low fibrinogen, bleeding, liver disease, DIC

sections.title: Acute Management
items: Airway: check for expanding neck/oropharyngeal bleed; intubate early if airway compromise is possible
Breathing: monitor SpO2 & WOB; treat hemothorax or pulmonary hemorrhage
Circulation: 2 largebore IVs, type & screen, CBC, coags, fibrinogen; activate MTP if life-threatening hemorrhage
Do NOT delay treatment while waiting for confirmatory factor levels if known or strongly suspected inherited bleeding disorder

sections.title: Chart Check / Hx.
items: Known diagnosis & type: Hemophilia A, Hemophilia B, vWD type 1, 2A, 2B, 2M, 2N, or 3
Baseline severity & home regimen: prophylactic factor, emicizumab use, prior DDAVP response, HumateP/Wilate/Vonvendi availability
Inhibitor history: prior factor VIII or IX inhibitor, bypassing agent use (rFVIIa or FEIBA)
Bleeding phenotype: hemarthrosis, deep muscle bleed, mucosal bleeding, epistaxis, menorrhagia, postpartum hemorrhage, procedurerelated bleeding
Timing & mechanism: spontaneous vs trauma vs postop/dental; head strike always matters
Medication review: aspirin, NSAIDs, anticoagulants, SSRIs, herbal supplements, recent DDAVP
Family history & prior abnl. procedures/extractions
Renal disease, CAD, pregnancy/postpartum status, & hyponatremia risk: se affect DDAVP safety

sections.title: Exam
items: Inspect for expanding hematoma, ecchymosis, hemarthrosis, compartment syndrome, & occult blood loss
Neuro exam if headache, trauma, or AMS: ICH can occult
Joint exam: warmth, swelling, ↓ ROM suggest hemarthrosis
Muscle groups/back/abdomen: deep bleeds can present with pain, neuropathy, or ↓ BP
Mucosal exam: epistaxis, gingival bleeding, oral cavity bleeding, menorrhagia severity
Airway/neck exam: tongue, retropharyngeal, or cervical hematoma

pairs.value: Factor VIII deficiency. Xlinked. Severity by factor level: severe <1%, moderate 1-5%, mild 5-40%.
Factor IX deficiency. Xlinked. Clinical bleeding pattern similar to Hemophilia A.
Partial quantitative vWF deficiency. Most common &mild;DDAVP responsive.
Qualitative vWF defect. 2A = loss of highmolecularweight multimers, 2B = increased platelet binding, 2M = defective platelet binding, 2N = low FVIII binding & may mimic mild Hemophilia A.
Nearcomplete vWF deficiency. Severe disease with mucosal & deep bleeding; DDAVPineffective.
Deep tissue bleeding, hemarthrosis, prolonged aPTT, low factor VIII. Consider acquired factor VIII inhibitor if no family history & severe unexplained bleeding.
Deep tissue bleeding, hemarthrosis, prolonged aPTT, low factor IX.
Mucosal bleeding, easy bruising, menorrhagia, procedurerelated bleeding; partial quantitative vWF deficiency.
Qualitative vWF disorders. 2N can look like mild Hemophilia A b/c factor VIII is low; multimer analysis & vWF studies distinguish m.
Enhanced platelet binding with thrombocytopenia risk; avoid DDAVP if suspected or known b/c it worsens thrombocytopenia
Severe inherited vWF deficiency; major mucosal & surgical bleeding, sometimes hemarthrosis b/c factor VIII canlow.
Mucosal bleeding with nl. PT/PTT may reflect platelet dysfunction, uremia, antiplatelet drugs, or thrombocytopenia.
Abnl. PT & PTT, low fibrinogen, thrombocytopenia, schistocytes, critical illness context.
Consider with new bleeding later in life, autoimmune disease, LVAD/aortic stenosis, lymphoproliferative disease, or isolated prolonged aPTT that does not correct.

sections.title: Management: Hemophilia A
items: Give recombinant factor VIII concentrate now for major bleeding; typical target FVIII activity 80-100% for life-threatening/CNS/neck/GI bleeding & 40-60% for less severe bleeds
If mild Hemophilia A & known DDAVP responder, DDAVP can used for minor bleeding or procedures; do NOT rely on DDAVP alone for major bleeding
If inhibitor history or poor response to factor VIII, use bypassing therapy (rFVIIa or FEIBA per hematology) instead of repeated ineffective FVIII dosing
Pts on emicizumab can still have breakthrough bleeding: coordinate with hematology before giving bypassing agents, especially FEIBA
Hemarthrosis or muscle bleed: factor first,thenrest/ice/compression/elevation & pain control; avoid NSAIDs

sections.title: Management: Hemophilia B
items: Give recombinant factor IX concentrate now for major bleeding; typical target FIX activity 60-100% depending on bleed severity & site
DDAVP is not useful in Hemophilia B
Because factor IX has longer halflife, repeat dosing unless frequent than factor VIII but still guided by bleed site, severity, & hematology
If known factor IX inhibitor or inadequate response, involve hematology urgently for bypassing therapy
Deep muscle, retroperitoneal, CNS, airway, & abdominal bleeds require admission & factor support even if initial symptoms improve

sections.title: Management: von Willebrand Disease
items: Type 1: DDAVP isfirst line if prior response is known or likely & bleeding is not life-threatening; monitor sodium & restrict free water
Type 2A & 2M: some pts respond to DDAVP, but many need vWFcontaining concentrate for significant bleeding or procedures
Type 2B: avoid DDAVP b/c it worsens thrombocytopenia; use vWFcontaining concentrate instead
Type 2N: may mimic mild Hemophilia A b/c FVIII is low; treat major bleeding with vWFcontaining concentrate not assuming isolated FVIII deficiency
Type 3: severe disease: DDAVP is ineffective; use vWFcontaining concentrate for major bleeding, surgery, & serious trauma

For all vWD types, add tranexamic acid for mucosal/oral/gynecologic bleeding when not contraindicated; escalate to vWFcontaining concentrate for major bleeding, failed DDAVP, pregnancy/postpartum hemorrhage, or invasive procedures

sections.title: Ongoing Management
items: Trend bleeding, hemoglobin, & product response; repeat factor levels if guided by hematology
Immobilize & ice hemarthrosis initially; avoid joint aspiration unless directed by specialists
Monitor sodium after DDAVP & restrict free water for 24h
For GI/intracranial/retroperitoneal bleeding or surgery, continue factor support beyond first dose based on site & severity
Documentproduct, dose, time, & response: this matters for repeat dosing & transfer
Before discharge, confirm access to home factor/vWF product, hematology follow up, & return precautions

pairs.value: CBC, type & screen, PT/INR, aPTT, fibrinogen, CMP;PT/PTT can nl. in mild vWD.
Factor VIII, factor IX, vWF antigen, vWF activity (ristocetin or GPIbbased), ± factor XI if needed.
Mixing study & Besda inhibitor assay.Don't wait for result before treating major bleed.
CT head for trauma/headache; CTA/CT as needed for neck, retroperitoneal, GI, or intramuscular bleeding.
Type & cross, serial hemoglobin, joint circumference/compartment checks, strict I&O if giving DDAVP.

drugs.name: Recombinant factor VIII
drugs.dose: Dose per hematology/product guide; typical major bleed target FVIII 80-100%
drugs.notes: Firstline for Hemophilia A major bleeding. If inhibitor present, may need bypassing agent instead.

drugs.name: Recombinant factor IX
drugs.dose: Dose per hematology/product guide; typical major bleed target FIX 60-100%
drugs.notes: Firstline for Hemophilia B major bleeding. Longer halflife than FVIII products.

drugs.name: vWFcontaining concentrate
drugs.dose: Per product guide (HumateP, Wilate, Vonvendibased strategy)
drugs.notes: Preferred for major vWD bleeding, type 3 disease, DDAVP nonresponse, or when DDAVP is contraindicated.

drugs.name: DDAVP (desmopressin)
drugs.dose: 0.3 mcg/kg IV over 20-30 min or 150-300 mcg IN depending on weight
drugs.contraindications: Type 2B vWD, significant hyponatremia risk, unstable CAD
drugs.notes: Useful for mild Hemophilia A & many type 1 vWD pts if known responder. Restrict free water & monitor sodium.

sections.title: Acute Management
items: Airway: check patency and protect. Breathing: check WOB, oxygenation, and ventilation. Circulation: check pulse, BP, perfusion, and IV access.
STOP transfusion now: clamp tubing, keep IV access open with NS
ABCs: check airway, breathing, hemodynamics. monitoring
Notify blood bank: save blood product bag & tubing for analysis
Draw: type & screen (new), DAT (Coombs), CBC, haptoglobin, LDH, bilirubin, free Hgb, fibrinogen
If anaphylaxis: IM epinephrine 0.3-0.5mg, IV fluids, Stop blood product
If TRALI: supportive care, O2, may need intubation & mechanical ventilation. Diuretics NOT helpful (noncardiogenic edema)
If TACO: sit upright, O2, furosemide 20-40mg IV, consider NIPPV. Volume overload: not permeability
If acute hemolytic: aggressive IVF (NS 200-300 mL/h) to maintain UOP >1 mL/kg/h, prevent renal failure from free Hgb. Send type & screen, DAT, hemolysis labs

pairs.value: Febrile nonhemolytic transfusion reaction: most common (1:300 pRBC, 1:10 plt). Temp ↑ ≥1°C during/after transfusion. Cytokinemed.. Dx of exclusion: must r/o hemolytic rxn & sepsis first
Transfusionassociated circulatory overload (1:700). Volume overload: pulm edema. HTN, ↑ JVP, ↑ BNP. Responds to diuretics. MCC of transfusionrelated death
Transfusionrelated acute lung injury (1:5,000). Noncardiogenic pulm edema within 6h of transfusion. ↓ BP, fever, bilateral infiltrates, nl BNP. Diuretics do NOT help: supportive care only
ABO incompatibility: medical emergency. Fever, flank pain, hemoglobinuria, DIC, renal failure, shock. Positive DAT. Mortality 5-10% if recognized early
Minor allergic (urticaria) = 1:100. Anaphylaxis = 1:40,000. IgAdeficient pts at highest risk of anaphylaxis. Treat with epi
Contaminated product: esp platelets (stored at room temp). High fever, rigors, ↓ BP, shock. Gram stain & culture of product

sections.title: Management
items: Stop the transfusion immediately, keep the IV open with normal saline, recheck pt and product identification, and notify the blood bank.
Send the remaining blood product plus post-reaction blood and urine samples for repeat type and screen, DAT, hemolysis evaluation, and culture when sepsis is a concern.
Acute hemolytic reaction: ICU plus renal support, aggressive isotonic fluids to maintain urine output, treat hyperkalemia, shock, and DIC, and send repeat ABO or crossmatch with full hemolysis labs.
FNHTR: exclude hemolysis and sepsis first, give acetaminophen or meperidine for rigors, and only resume transfusion if evaluation is negative and symptoms fully resolve.

Allergic reaction: pause for urticaria and give diphenhydramine; for bronchospasm, hypotension, or airway edema, stop permanently and treat as anaphylaxis with IM epinephrine plus oxygen, IV fluids, bronchodilator, antihistamines, and steroids.
TACO: stop transfusion, sit upright, give oxygen, and diurese; think hypertension, positive fluid balance, elevated BNP or CVP, and pulmonary edema on chest x-ray.

TRALI: stop transfusion and give supportive respiratory care with oxygen or lung-protective ventilation; avoid diuretics and distinguish from TACO by normal or low BNP or CVP and more frequent hypotension.

Delayed hemolytic reaction: confirm with DAT or antibody testing and hemolysis labs; avoid further transfusion if possible, use extended antigen-matched blood if transfusion is unavoidable, and treat severe hyperhemolysis with hematology-guided steroids plus IVIG and possible complement blockade.
Septic transfusion reaction: stop transfusion, start broad-spectrum antibiotics immediately, get pt and product cultures, and manage as sepsis with fluids and vasopressors if needed.

topics.title: Acute Chest Syndrome
topics.subtitle: Chest pain, fever, hypoxemia, infiltrate, sickle cell disease

sections.title: Acute Management
items: Airway: check patency and protect. Breathing: check WOB, oxygenation, and ventilation. Circulation: check pulse, BP, perfusion, and IV access.
ABCs: O2 to maintain SpO2 ≥95%. monitoring. Largebore IV access
Simple transfusion: target Hgb 10 g/dL (do NOT exceed: ↑ viscosity). For moderate ACS without rapid decline
Exchange transfusion (automated erythrocytapheresis): for severe ACS (SpO2 <90% despite O2, multilobar infiltrates, rapid deterioration, HgbS >30%). Target HgbS <30%, Hgb ~10
Bronchodilators (albuterol neb q4-6h): if wheezing or reactive airway component
Avoid excessive O2 (rebound sickling when removed), excessive IVF, transfusion to Hgb >10

sections.title: Chart Check / Hx.
items: Sickle cell genotype: HbSS (most severe), HbSC, HbSbeta thal
Baseline Hgb & HgbS% (for transfusion targets)
Triggers: VOC (vasoocclusive crisis): ACS is most common complication of hospitalized VOC pts. Also: infection, fat embolism from bone marrow necrosis, PE, postop (esp Abd/chest surgery)
Hydroxyurea use & compliance (↓ ACS episodes)
Prior ACS episodes: frequency, severity, prior exchange transfusions
Alloimmunization status: sickle pts develop alloantibodies from frequent transfusions: need extended phenotypematched blood
Iron overload status (chronic transfusions)
Recent surgery, anesthesia (↑ ACS risk postop)

sections.title: Exam
items: Fever + new pulmonary infiltrate + respiratory sx in sickle cell pt = ACS until proven otherwise
Respiratory: tachypnea, ↓ SpO2, crackles, wheezing, ↓ breath sounds, pleuritic chest pain
Fever (common: does not differentiate infection from infarction)
Pain: chest wall, rib, sternal: distinguish from VOC pain vs new ACS
Abd: splinting from pain, hepatomegaly, RUQ tenderness (hepatic sequestration)
Signs of worsening anemia: pallor, tachycardia, fatigue, jaundice (hemolysis)
Neuro: AMS, focal deficits (concurrent stroke: can cooccur with ACS)

pairs.value: New pulmonary infiltrate on CXR + ≥1 of: fever (>38.5°C), chest pain, respiratory sx (cough, dyspnea, tachypnea, ↓ SpO2) in sickle cell pt
Vasoocclusion in pulmonary vasculature + infection + fat embolism from bone marrow necrosis: V/Q mismatch, atelectasis, infarction: cycle of sickling
ACS is #1 cause of death in sickle cell dz & #1 cause of ICU admission
Automated erythrocytapheresis: removes HgbS cells & replaces with HgbA. Target HgbS <30%, Hgb ~10. Avoids hyperviscosity
Most common identifiable cause (~30%). Atypicals (Mycoplasma, Chlamydia) + typical bacteria (S. pneumo, H. flu)
From bone marrow necrosis during VOC. Leads to lung injury & ACS
In situ thrombosis / vasoocclusion in pulm vasculature
Rib/chest wall pain from VOC: splinting: atelectasis: ACS. Why IS q2h is critical
PNA (overlap), PE, VOC without ACS (no infiltrate), ARDS, heart failure, fat embolism syndrome, pulm hemorrhage

sections.title: Management
items: Start empiric abx: ceftriaxone 2g IV + azithromycin 500mg IV/PO to cover typical + atypical triggers
Control pain aggressively & use incentive spirometry q2h while awake: pain/splinting drives atelectasis & worsens ACS
Give judicious IVF only; avoid overhydration. Add albuterol if wheezing or reactive airway component is present
Escalate transfusion based on severity: simple transfusion for moderate ACS, exchange transfusion for severe hypoxemia, multilobar disease, or rapid decline
Add supportive care: DVT prophylaxis, repeat CXR/oxygen assessment, & ICUlevel monitoring if worsening

Hgb (↓ from baseline: transfusion threshold), reticulocyte count, WBC
HgbS%: guides exchange transfusion (target <30%)
Extended phenotype match: sickle pts have high alloimmunization rates
Hemolysis markers, renal function

If PE suspected (can coexist). Incidental finding of in situ thrombosis common in SCD

topics.title: Immune Thrombocytopenia (ITP)
topics.subtitle: Petechiae, mucosal bleeding, severe thrombocytopenia, otherwise normal coagulation

sections.title: Acute Management
items: Airway: check patency and protect. Breathing: check WOB, oxygenation, and ventilation. Circulation: check pulse, BP, perfusion, and IV access.
check for life-threatening bleeding: ICH, GI hemorrhage, mucosal hemorrhage, hemodynamic instability
Type & screen, crossmatch if surgical intervention possible
If critical bleeding or plt <10,000 with active bleeding: platelet transfusion (even though consumed rapidly) + IVIG 1g/kg IV + methylprednisolone 1g IV daily x3 days + consider TXA

sections.title: Chart Check / Hx.
items: New vs chronic ITP (new: <3 months, persistent: 3-12 months, chronic: >12 months)
Meds: heparin ( r/o HIT), quinine, sulfonamides, vancomycin, GPIIb/IIIa inhibitors, vaccines
Recent infections: viral URI, HIV, HCV, H. pylori, CMV, EBV
Autoimmune dz: SLE (lupus), antiphospholipid syndrome, CLL, lymphoma
Pregnancy (gestational thrombocytopenia vs ITP vs HELLP vs TTP)
Prior plt counts: sudden ↓ vs chronic low baseline
Bleeding hx: mucocutaneous (petechiae, purpura, gingival bleeding, menorrhagia, epistaxis), GI, hematuria, ICH
Prior treatments for ITP: steroids, IVIG, antiD, splenectomy, TPO agonists
Family hx of bleeding disorders

sections.title: Exam
items: Mucocutaneous bleeding pattern: petechiae, purpura, ecchymoses (nonpalpable: palpable purpura: think vasculitis/TTP)
Wet purpura: blood blisters in oral mucosa: marker of severe disease & ↑ ICH risk
Gingival bleeding, epistaxis, menorrhagia
Splenomegaly: absence expected in ITP: if spleen palpable, consider or dx (lymphoma, liver dz, splenic sequestration)
Signs of underlying cause: lymphadenopathy (lymphoma), malar rash (SLE), hepatomegaly (liver dz)
Neuro exam: headache, AMS, focal deficits: r/o ICH (CT head now)
No joint hemarthroses or deep tissue bleeds (that's coagulation factor deficiency, not platelet disorder)

pairs.value: Immunemed. platelet destruction: autoantibodies (usually antiGPIIb/IIIa) target platelets for splenic destruction. Dx of exclusion: r/o or causes of thrombocytopenia
<10,000: spontaneous bleeding risk (esp ICH). <20,000: tx indicated. <30,000: tx if bleeding or procedure. >30,000 + no bleeding: may observe
Blood blisters in oral mucosa. Marker of severe ITP with ↑ risk of ICH. Warrants aggressive tx
Primary: isolated thrombocytopenia, no identifiable cause. Secondary: from underlying condition (SLE, HIV, HCV, drugs, lymphoma)

TTP/HUS (MAHA + thrombocytopenia + AKI/neuro sx), HIT (plt ↓ 5-10d after heparin), DIC (↑ PT/INR, ↓ fibrinogen), drug induced, bone marrow failure, splenic sequestration, pseudothrombocytopenia (EDTA artifact: check citrated tube)
SLE, antiphospholipid syndrome, HIV, HCV, H. pylori, CLL, lymphoma, common variable immunodeficiency, postvaccine
↓ Production: bone marrow failure, chemo, radiation, B12/folate deficiency, MDS. ↑ Destruction: ITP, TTP/HUS, HIT, DIC. Sequestration: hypersplenism, cirrhosis. Dilutional: massive transfusion
ITP: isolated plt ↓, nl. smear (or ↑ megakaryocytes). TTP: MAHA (schistocytes), ↑ LDH, ↓ haptoglobin. DIC: ↑ PT, ↓ fibrinogen. HIT: 5-10d postheparin

sections.title: Management
items: First decide if this is critical bleeding, noncritical bleeding, or isolated thrombocytopenia
If critical bleeding: give platelets + IVIG + high dose steroids now, hold anticoagulants/antiplatelets, & control the bleed source
If plt <30,000 with significant but nonlife-threatening bleeding: start dexamethasone 40mg PO/IV daily x4 days preferred, or prednisone 1 mg/kg/day
If plt <20,000-30,000 without bleeding: treat with corticosteroids; if plt >30,000 & no bleeding or planned procedure: observation may reasonable
Avoid IM injections, rectal exams, & unnecessary procedures while platelets arelow

nl. (unless bleeding)
nl. in ITP: if abnl., consider DIC, liver dz, or coagulopathy
Mandatory: r/o schistocytes (TTP), blasts (leukemia), pseudothrombocytopenia (clumps)
r/o hemolysis (TTP/HUS/Evans syndrome)
If anemia present: Evans syndrome = ITP + AIHA
Screen all new ITP pts: secondary causes that change management

drugs.notes: Preferred first line over prednisone: faster plt response, shorter course. Plt rise in 2-4 days. Can repeat cycles

drugs.name: Prednisone
drugs.dose: 1 mg/kg/day PO (max 80mg) x2-4 wks, then taper
drugs.notes: Alternative to dexamethasone. Slower response, longer course, more side effects from prolonged use

drugs.name: IVIG
drugs.notes: For life-threatening bleeding or preprocedure. Rapid plt rise in 24-48h (faster than steroids). Temporary effect (2-4 wks). Combine with steroids

drugs.name: Platelet transfusion
drugs.contraindications: Avoid if not actively bleeding (consumed rapidly, rarely effective alone)
drugs.notes: Only for life-threatening bleeding in ITP. Consumedbut provides transient hemostasis. Always combine with IVIG + steroids

drugs.name: Tranexamic acid (TXA)
drugs.contraindications: Active intravascular clotting, hematuria from upper urinary tract
drugs.notes: Adjunct for mucosal bleeding (epistaxis, menorrhagia, GI). Antifibrinolytic

drugs.notes: Alternative antifibrinolytic to TXA for mucosal bleeding

topics.title: TMA / TTP / HUS
topics.subtitle: MAHA, thrombocytopenia, AKI, neuro changes, hemolysis labs

sections.title: Acute Management
items: Airway: check patency and protect. Breathing: check WOB, oxygenation, and ventilation. Circulation: check pulse, BP, perfusion, and IV access.
Plasma exchange (PLEX): definitive tx. Contact blood bank/apheresis team IMMEDIATELY.Don't wait for ADAMTS13 results
Do NOT transfuse platelets: worsens microvascular thrombosis & organ damage. Exception: life-threatening bleeding only
IVF, monitor UOP, check Cr q6-12h (renal involvement)

sections.title: Chart Check / Hx.
items: Acute onset: AMS, petechiae/purpura, fatigue, dark urine, ↓ UOP, Abd pain
Preceding diarrhea (bloody: Shiga toxin HUS: E. coli O157:H7, Shigella)
meds: quinine, calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus, cyclosporine), gemcitabine, bevacizumab, ticlopidine, clopidogrel
Pregnancy / postpartum (TTP, HELLP, preeclampsia overlap)
HIV, autoimmune dz (SLE: secondary TMA)
Transplant: BMT or solid organ (calcineurin inhibitor toxicity)
Recurrent TTP episodes (relapsing acquired TTP: may need rituximab)
Family hx (congenital TTP: UpshawSchulman syndrome, hereditary ADAMTS13 deficiency)

sections.title: Exam
items: Classic TTP pentad (FAT RN): Fever, Anemia (MAHA), Thrombocytopenia, Renal dysfunction, Neurologic sx. All 5 rarely present: do NOT wait for full pentad
Neuro: AMS, headache, seizures, focal deficits, visual changes, coma ( present in ~60%)
Skin: petechiae, purpura, jaundice (hemolysis)
Renal: ↓ UOP, edema, HTN (more prominent in HUS)
Abd: pain, N/V, bloody diarrhea (Shigatoxin HUS)
Cardiac: chest pain, arrhythmia (myocardial microthrombi: underrecognized cause of death)
Pallor, tachycardia, fatigue (severe anemia from MAHA)

pairs.value: Thrombotic microangiopathy: umbrella term for MAHA + thrombocytopenia + organ damage from microvascular thrombosis. Includes TTP, HUS, & or causes
Acquired autoimmune (antiADAMTS13 antibodies) or congenital (UpshawSchulman). ADAMTS13 <10% = TTP. Deficiency: ultralarge vWF multimers: platelet microthrombi
Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia: schistocytes on smear (fragmented RBCs), ↑ LDH, ↓ haptoglobin, ↑ indirect bilirubin, negative DAT
Typical HUS: bloody diarrhea: E. coli O157:H7 or Shigella. Mainly pediatric. Supportive care only: PLEX & abx NOT beneficial. Avoid antidiarrheals
Complementmed. TMA. Primarily renal. Tx: eculizumab (antiC5 monoclonal ab). PLEX is bridge only
Predicts ADAMTS13 <10%. Score <5 = effectively r/o TTP (99% NPV). Factors: plt <30K, hemolysis, no cancer, no transplant, MCV <90, INR <1.5, Cr <2.0
Acquired autoimmune (most common adult TMA), congenital ADAMTS13 deficiency (UpshawSchulman), pregnancyassociated
Shigatoxin (E. coli O157, Shigella), complementmed. (aHUS), drug induced
Calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus, cyclosporine), quinine, gemcitabine, bevacizumab, mitomycin C, ticlopidine
TTP, HUS, DIC (↑ PT, ↓ fibrinogen), HELLP syndrome, malignant HTN, scleroderma renal crisis, catastrophic APLS, prosthetic valve hemolysis, disseminated cancer
TTP: nl. PT/INR & fibrinogen. DIC: ↑ PT/INR, ↓ fibrinogen, ↑ Ddimer. Both have MAHA & thrombocytopenia
TTP: neuro predominant, ADAMTS13 <10%. HUS: renal predominant, ± bloody diarrhea, ADAMTS13 nl.

sections.title: General TMA Management
items: MAHA + thrombocytopenia = TTP until proven otherwise while you send confirmatory studies
Stop potential triggers: quinine, calcineurin inhibitors, gemcitabine, bevacizumab, clopidogrel / ticlopidine, offending chemo or transplant meds
Support endorgan perfusion: isotonic IVF if not overloaded, strict I&Os, telemetry, serial CBC / LDH / Cr
RBC transfusion is appropriate for symptomatic anemia; avoid platelet transfusion unless life-threatening hemorrhage or urgent procedure
Involve hematology early for all suspected TMAs, plus nephrology if AKI / dialysis risk & blood bank / apheresis if TTP remains on table

sections.title: TTP Management
items: If TTP suspected: treat empirically: mortality >90% untreatedDon't wait for ADAMTS13 result
Start PLEX now & continue daily until plt >150K for 2 days & hemolysis resolves
Give steroids: methylprednisolone 1g IV daily x3 days, then prednisone 1mg/kg/day
Add caplacizumab 11mg IV before first PLEX, then 11mg SC daily after each PLEX & continue 30 days after PLEX completion
If PLEX is delayed, give FFP 15-30 mL/kg as bridge after drawing ADAMTS13 & inhibitor studies
Consider rituximab early for refractory, relapsing, autoimmune, or severe disease with slow platelet recovery

sections.title: Shigatoxin HUS Management
items: Supportive care is definitive tx. Careful isotonic IVF early, monitor UOP, daily weights, electrolytes, CBC, LDH, & Cr
Avoid antibiotics & antimotility agents in suspected enterohemorrhagic E. coli: may increase toxin exposure & worsen HUS
Manage complications: transfuse RBCs for symptomatic anemia, treat severe HTN, correct electrolytes, & start dialysis if needed
Do NOT use routine PLEX or eculizumab for typical Shigatoxin HUS unless another TMA phenotype is emerging
Escalate level of care for worsening AKI, encephalopathy, severe colitis, fluid overload, or dialysis need

sections.title: Atypical HUS Management
items: Suspect aHUS when renalpredominant TMA has nl. / nearnl. ADAMTS13 & no convincing Shigatoxin trigger
Start eculizumab (or ravulizumab if your center has it per local protocol) as definitive complement blockade once meningococcal prophylaxis plan is addressed
PLEX is not definitive for aHUS, but may used only as a temporary bridge while diagnosis is clarified & complement inhibition is arranged
Involve nephrology early: many pts need dialysis support & close renal recovery monitoring
Screen for complementmed. / secondary triggers: pregnancy, transplant, infection, autoimmune disease, malignant HTN, & offending meds

pairs.value: <10% = TTP. 10-20% = equivocal. >20% = not TTP. Draw BEFORE starting PLEX. Also send ADAMTS13 inhibitor/antibody
Calculate now: plt <30K, hemolysis markers, no active cancer, no transplant, MCV <90, INR <1.5, Cr <2.0. Score <5 effectively r/o TTP
Schistocytes (fragmented RBCs): hallmark of MAHA. Also: polychromasia, ↓ plt
↑↑ LDH (often >1000), ↓↓ haptoglobin (often undetectable), ↑ indirect bilirubin, ↑ reticulocytes, negative DAT
PT/INR & fibrinogen nl. in TTP. If abnl.: think DIC
Renal function: AKI more prominent in HUS
Shiga toxin PCR / E. coli O157 culture if bloody diarrhea
C3, C4, Factor H, Factor I: if aHUS suspected
Cardiac microthrombi: underrecognized cause of mortality

drugs.name: Plasma exchange (PLEX)
drugs.dose: 1-1.5 plasma volumes daily until plt >150K x2 days + LDH returning to normal
drugs.contraindications: None absolute in TTP (lifesaving). Hemodynamic instability (relative)
drugs.notes: Definitive tx for TTP. Removes antiADAMTS13 antibodies & ultralarge vWF multimers. Replaces with donor ADAMTS13. Start ASAP —don't wait for ADAMTS13 result

drugs.name: Methylprednisolone (pulse)
drugs.dose: 1g IV daily x3 days, then prednisone 1mg/kg/day PO
drugs.notes: Suppresses autoantibody production. Start concurrent with PLEX

drugs.name: Caplacizumab
drugs.dose: 11mg IV bolus (before first PLEX), then 11mg SC daily (after each PLEX) + 30 days after PLEX series ends
drugs.notes: AntivWF nanobody: blocks plateletvWF interaction. ↓ Thrombotic events, ↓ exacerbations, ↓ time to plt recovery. ↑ Bleeding risk: monitor closely

drugs.name: Rituximab
drugs.notes: For refractory or relapsing TTP. Depletes antiADAMTS13 antibodyproducing B cells. Takes 1-2 wks for effect

drugs.name: FFP (fresh frozen plasma)
drugs.notes: Bridge only until PLEX available. Provides ADAMTS13 enzyme. Not substitute for PLEX

drugs.name: Eculizumab
drugs.dose: 900mg IV weekly x4 wks, then 1200mg q2wks
drugs.contraindications: Unvaccinated for meningococcus (must vaccinate + prophylactic abx)
drugs.notes: For atypical HUS (complementmed.). AntiC5 monoclonal antibody. Not for TTP or Shigatoxin HUS

topics.title: HLH
topics.subtitle: Fever, cytopenias, hepatosplenomegaly, hyperferritinemia, multiorgan failure

sections.title: Acute Management
items: Airway: check patency and protect. Breathing: check WOB, oxygenation, and ventilation. Circulation: check pulse, BP, perfusion, and IV access.
ABCs: many pts need ICU (MV/pressors in ~70% of ICU admissions)
Stat labs: CBC, CMP, ferritin, fibrinogen, triglycerides, LDH, sCD25 (sIL2R), Ddimer
Lifethreatening hyperinflammatory emergency: high mortality if untreated

sections.title: Chart Check / Hx.
items: Known malignancy (esp lymphoma: 76% of malignant triggers), recent chemo/immunothetherapy
Autoimmune dz (SLE = 39% of autoimmune triggered HLH; sJIA, AOSD)
Recent infections: EBV (worst viral prognosis, 5yr survival 25%), CMV, HIV
Immunodeficiency, transplant history, immunosuppressant use
Family hx: consanguinity, infant deaths, primary HLH (median onset 3–6 months)
CART or bispecific Ab thetherapy (CRS: HLH overlap)

sections.title: Exam
items: Persistent fever (≥38.5°C) unresponsive to abx
Hepatosplenomegaly (common; unusual in sepsis: distinguishing feature)
Lymphadenopathy
Petechiae, purpura, maculopapular rash
Jaundice, RUQ tenderness (hepatic involvement in ~60% adults)
Neuro: AMS, seizures, ataxia, meningism (~1/3 at dx; ↑ mortality)
Signs of multiorgan failure: pulmonary, renal, GI

pairs.value: Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis: overwhelming immune activation with uncontrolled macrophage/Tcell proliferation: cytokine storm: multiorgan failure
Inherited defects in cytotoxic lymphocyte function (PRF1, UNC13D, STX11, STXBP2). Mainly infants. Requires HSCT for cure
Acquired; triggered by infection, malignancy, or autoimmune dz. Adults: mean age ~50, M:F 1.7:1
Macrophage activation syndrome: form of secondary HLH in autoimmune dz (SLE, sJIA, AOSD)

Need ≥5/8: fever ≥38.5°C, splenomegaly, bicytopenia (Hb <90, plt <100, ANC <1.0), hypertriglyceridemia (≥3.0 mmol/L) or hypofibrinogenemia (≤1.5 g/L), hemophagocytosis on biopsy, ferritin ≥500, ↓/absent NK activity, sCD25 ≥2400 U/mL. 4 criteria = 95% sensitivity, 94% specificity
Weighted scoring (0–337) using 9 variables. Score ≥168 = 100% sensitivity, 94% specificity. Better validated for adults
EBV (most common viral), CMV, HIV, adenovirus, bacterial sepsis. EBVHLH: 5yr survival only 25%
Lymphoma (76% of malignant triggers), esp T/NKcell, AITL, intravascular DLBCL. sCD25:ferritin ratio ≥2.0 = 85% PPV for lymphomaHLH. Worst prognosis (20–30% 2yr survival)
SLE (39%), sJIA, AOSD. AOSD:high CRP, IL18 >18,550 pg/mL (90% Sn, 94% Sp vs HLH)
Shares fever, cytopenias, MOF. HLH distinguished by: hepatosplenomegaly, hypofibrinogenemia, hypertriglyceridemia, markedly ↑ sCD25, CD38²⁰/HLADR+ >7% of CD8+ Tcells
Spiking fever, rash, arthralgia, ↑↑ ferritin. CRP >130 + sCD25 <3900 = 91% Sn/93% Sp for AOSD vs HLH
DIC, TTP, MODS, histiocytic malignancies, inborn errors of metabolism (infants)

sections.title: Management
items: Check ferritin early: it is almost always elevated; >500 supports HLH and >10,000 is more specific in adults.
Apply HLH-2004 criteria or an adult HScore; send sCD25, NK-cell activity, and perforin or CD107a flow cytometry when appropriate.
Identify the trigger immediately: infection, malignancy, rheumatologic disease or MAS, or familial or genetic HLH.
Give ICU-level supportive care when organ dysfunction, respiratory failure, or shock is present; start empiric antimicrobials if infection is possible and support cytopenias or coagulopathy.
If disease is severe or progressive, start immunomodulation while the workup continues: high-dose methylprednisolone 10-30 mg/kg/day (max 1 g) or dexamethasone 10 mg/m²/day.
Add anakinra 2-10 mg/kg/day early when suspicion remains high; IVIG 1-2 g/kg is another adjunct when appropriate.
Primary or familial HLH usually needs an HLH-2004-type regimen with etoposide, dexamethasone, and cyclosporine as a bridge to HSCT.
Secondary HLH may respond to glucocorticoids with or without IVIG or anakinra, but severe, progressive, or CNS disease should prompt etoposide-based therapy.
check for CNS involvement and do not delay systemic treatment for MRI or LP; intrathecal methotrexate plus corticosteroids may be needed when CNS disease is confirmed.
Trend clinical status daily and ferritin, CBC, LFTs, coagulation studies, and triglycerides at least twice weekly; worsening ferritin, cytopenias, hepatitis, or DIC means recheck and escalate.
For refractory disease, discuss emapalumab, ruxolitinib, or alemtuzumab with hematology.
Consult hematology or oncology urgently and involve rheumatology, infectious disease, critical care, and HSCT teams early.

pairs.value: CBC with diff, CMP, LDH, ferritin, fibrinogen, triglycerides, Ddimer, PT/PTT, CRP, lactate
sCD25 (sIL2R), CXCL9, NK cell activity, flow cytometry (perforin, CD107a degranulation). IL18 if AOSD suspected
EBV PCR, CMV PCR, adenovirus PCR, HIV, blood cultures, fungal markers (if immunosuppressed)
Aspirate preferred over biopsy (84% vs 64% sensitivity for hemophagocytosis). R/o malignancy. May be absent early
CT C/A/P (r/o malignancy, occult infection). FDGPET if lymphoma suspected (may present without discrete lesions on CT)
Brain MRI (multifocal WM lesions, cerebellar involvement) + CSF analysis (cell count, protein, glucose) if neuro sx, age <1 yr, or known genetic dz
NGS panel or WES early in pediatric cases or young adults. Flow for perforin/CD107a for rapid screening

drugs.name: Methylprednisolone
drugs.notes: Firstline per EULAR/ACR 2022. Alt: dexamethasone 10 mg/m²/d (better CNS penetration).

drugs.name: Anakinra
drugs.notes: IL1RA. Early immunomodulation with minimal immunosuppression. Favorable safety at high doses.

drugs.name: Etoposide
drugs.notes: For severe/refractory dz or CNS involvement. Ageadjusted dosing. Core of HLH94/2004 protocols.

drugs.name: Cyclosporine
drugs.notes: Part of HLH2004 protocol for primary HLH. Monitor levels, renal function.

drugs.name: Emapalumab
drugs.notes: AntiIFNγ mAb. FDAapproved for primary HLH. 57% preHSCT survival in refractory dz.

drugs.name: IVIG
drugs.notes: Immunomodulatory adjunct. May be used early alongside steroids.
